accuracy_reason: Man as the image of the image (Christ being the image of God) is an old patristic idea. Burton's following English does explain it rather than translate it.
usefulness_reason: Points to the theological background, but thinly; it does not name the source or say that Christ is the first image.

accuracy_reason: Summum genus is correctly defined as the most general class in the scholastic (Porphyrian) scheme.
usefulness_reason: Explains a technical logical term that Burton uses to place dotage above the other species of madness.

accuracy_reason: The etymology is right. Aristotle names epichairekakia among passions bad in themselves (NE 2.6, 1107a; also 2.7). Burton's gloss does add grieving at others' prosperity.
usefulness_reason: Gives the word's makeup and its Aristotelian background, which a reader would not otherwise have.

accuracy_reason: The note is right. Burton's 'pro and con' is the English phrase taken from Latin 'pro et contra', meaning for and against.
usefulness_reason: The note only restates the translation and the familiar English phrase, so a reader learns nothing new from it.

accuracy_reason: It is indeed the title of a tract that Burton cites.
usefulness_reason: Only labels the phrase as a title and says nothing about the work or its author.

accuracy_reason: 'Caepit' is an early-modern spelling of 'coepit', and 'delirare' does mean to rave or dote.
usefulness_reason: A spelling and vocabulary note that the translation and Burton's own gloss already cover.

accuracy_reason: The sidenote does go on to cite Boissardus, book 1. 'De praestig.' points to his work on magical illusions (De divinatione et magicis praestigiis).
usefulness_reason: Expands the cut-off reference, which helps a little, but it is mostly about where the marked passage ends.

accuracy_reason: Innatae is an adjective going with 'causes', and Burton does gloss the three Latin terms as 'inward, innate, and inbred'.
usefulness_reason: A grammar note repeating Burton's own gloss.

accuracy_reason: A popina was a cookshop or low eating-house, and the phrase is scornful.
usefulness_reason: Gives the sense of popina and the tone of the phrase, but does not locate it in Seneca.

accuracy_reason: The sidenote sits at 'slaves' in the main text, and Burton's English takes up only 'mancipia'.
usefulness_reason: A working remark on how the sidenote lines up with the text; it adds nothing on the Seneca passage.

accuracy_reason: The citation does refer to Egnatius (Giovanni Battista Egnazio), who wrote on and annotated the lives of the emperors. The main text names him.
usefulness_reason: Identifies the reference in a general way, but does not specify which of Egnatius's works is meant.

accuracy_reason: Understanding 'drink' as the object fits Pliny NH 14. But the claim that the sentence goes on in item 1.2.2.2-f96 cannot be confirmed; the continuation 'ut magna pars…' follows straight on in the text, and the numbering gap looks odd.
usefulness_reason: A grammar note plus an editorial cross-reference, with nothing on the Pliny context.

accuracy_reason: Philippians 3:19 reads 'quorum Deus venter est' in the Vulgate; this is clearly the allusion.
usefulness_reason: It identifies the biblical allusion behind Burton's tag.

accuracy_reason: In humoral medicine 'crude' means unconcocted, or undigested.
usefulness_reason: It glosses a technical term, but the main text already says 'raw, and as yet undigested'.

accuracy_reason: De officiis 3.1 reads 'numquam se minus otiosum esse quam cum otiosus, nec minus solum quam cum solus esset'. That is indirect speech with the leisure clause first, as the note says.
usefulness_reason: It is an accurate comparison with the source, but the reader gains little from it.

accuracy_reason: Tellus is the Roman personified Earth goddess.
usefulness_reason: The gloss is correct but slight. It misses that in Hyginus Tellus also claims the right to name the creature.

accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 412 reads 'Qui studet optatam cursu contingere metam'.
usefulness_reason: It notes a small verbal variant and does not name the work. This is close to a textual working note.

accuracy_reason: The saying is proverbial. Its classical source is Sallust, Jugurtha 8.1 ('Romae omnia venalia esse') and 35.10, which the note does not mention, though nothing it says is false.
usefulness_reason: It mostly repeats what Burton says and misses the Sallust source a reader would want.

accuracy_reason: 'iisdem pro arbitrio abutentes' has no equivalent of 'make them say what they propose'. The phrase is Burton's addition.
usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton slants his own paraphrase, which is mildly interesting.

accuracy_reason: 'indigna quae vel recipiantur in triviis' does end the preceding clause, and haras/aras is a deliberate wordplay.
usefulness_reason: Pointing out the pun helps a little, but most of the note explains the construction.

accuracy_reason: The continuation 'putidi dicterium de clero usurpare' is quoted correctly, and the gloss is reasonable.
usefulness_reason: It is a construal and translation note. It does not say that the 'rank jibe' is Campion's, as the sidenote indicates.

accuracy_reason: Persius 3.85 reads 'hoc est quod palles? cur quis non prandeat hoc est?', and it mocks the pale, fasting philosopher.
usefulness_reason: It gives the original context and shows how Burton turns the line on divines.

accuracy_reason: In Alciato's emblem on poverty holding back talent, 'Ut me pluma levat' is line 2 and 'Ingenio poteram' is line 3. Burton reverses them and leaves out the rest of the emblem.
usefulness_reason: It names the emblem, describes its image and says how Burton cuts and reorders it.

accuracy_reason: The guess about the sense is hedged with 'perhaps', and Burton does credit 'Austin'. However, Augustine's analogy is about many small sins, so the 'vermin in the body' reading is a speculative guess.
usefulness_reason: These are mostly translation working notes, and the attribution only repeats the main text.

accuracy_reason: Burton's English does expand 'publica hilaritas' into 'all good fellowship, peace, mirth, and plenty'.
usefulness_reason: It points out a small freedom in Burton's gloss, but a reader loses little without it.

accuracy_reason: Leonardo Loredan was Doge from 1501 to 1521, so he held office during the War of the League of Cambrai. Bembo records the herald's address to him in the Senate.
usefulness_reason: It names the Doge and explains whose words these are, which the reader needs.

accuracy_reason: 'corum' makes no sense in Latin, and 'eorum' fits both the sense and the translation.
usefulness_reason: This is a textual or misprint note, a translator's working note.

accuracy_reason: 'Per consensum' (sympathy, consent of parts) is a standard term of Galenic medicine, and here it is applied to body and soul.
usefulness_reason: It explains a technical medical term.

accuracy_reason: Gellius 13.11 gives Varro's Menippean satire the title 'Nescis quid vesper serus vehat', and Georgics 1.461 has 'quid vesper serus vehat'. The other claims are also correct.
usefulness_reason: It gives the proverb's source and shows how Burton changes the wording.

accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 7–8 reads 'velut aegri somnia, vanae / fingentur species'.
usefulness_reason: The variant is correct, but it does not even name the poem, so it is slight.

accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.3.11–12, says of Tigellius 'habebat saepe ducentos, saepe decem servos' as an example of his inconsistency.
usefulness_reason: It identifies 'the Poet' and the figure meant, and it explains the point of the allusion.

accuracy_reason: The Latin is grammatically loose, and the main text does say 'of what complexion the part is, of black or red'.
usefulness_reason: It notes a minor difference between the sidenote and Burton's paraphrase.

accuracy_reason: These are rare Tertullianic words, and Burton's main text has 'imbonities, insuavities'.
usefulness_reason: It explains Burton's odd English words, but only slightly.

accuracy_reason: The line is the last line of Martial 10.47, not Horace.
usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's misattribution and gives the true source.

accuracy_reason: διαιτητική is the art of regimen, or dietetics.
usefulness_reason: It mostly repeats the translation.

accuracy_reason: Kepler wrote the Somnium (published 1634) and the Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo (1610), his reply to Galileo.
usefulness_reason: It expands Burton's cryptic abbreviations into the two works and gives their context.

accuracy_reason: Naulum is the Greek-derived word for a passage fee, the coin paid to Charon for the ferry.
usefulness_reason: A correct gloss, but Burton's own 'no fees to be paid' and his mention of Charon already make the sense clear.

accuracy_reason: Burton's Latin does run on into 'stili tantum & ingenii causa'. Cunaeus's disclaimer echoes Lucian, True History 1.4, where Lucian says he will write of things that neither are nor could be.
usefulness_reason: The link to Lucian's True History shows the reader what kind of joke Cunaeus is making.

accuracy_reason: The passage is from Seneca, Natural Questions 7.25 (on comets), which has 'tam rarum mundi spectaculum' and no 'fortasse'. Burton's 'cap. 35' does not match that numbering.
usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and shows how Burton changes and shortens it, adding 'perhaps' and turning Seneca's point toward God's providence.

accuracy_reason: 'Without book' did mean 'by heart, from memory' in early modern English.
usefulness_reason: A small but helpful gloss on an old English phrase; the translation already says 'by heart'.

accuracy_reason: Burton means Roger Bacon's Epistola de secretis operibus artis et naturae. The machines Burton lists (a chariot moving without animals, flying devices) come from that letter.
usefulness_reason: It names the actual work Burton cites and its full title.

accuracy_reason: Burton's English on either side of the Latin does give its sense.
usefulness_reason: It only repeats what the translation and Burton's own English already say.

accuracy_reason: The source (Velleius 2.107: an old German visits Tiberius on the Elbe) is right. But 'dies' can be feminine in Latin, so it is too strong to say 'ullam' does not agree with 'diem'.
usefulness_reason: It points out that Burton misremembers the source, putting Caesar and the Rhine in place of Tiberius and the Elbe.

accuracy_reason: Valescus de Taranta was a Montpellier physician who was active around 1380–1420; his Philonium dates from 1418.
usefulness_reason: A brief identification of the author; useful, but slight.

accuracy_reason: The grammar it describes is right: the phrase means he went even though he himself shrank from it.
usefulness_reason: This is a grammar note for the translator, not for the reader.

accuracy_reason: The saying is Publilius Syrus's, and it usually reads 'Comes facundus in via pro vehiculo est'.
usefulness_reason: It names the source of the proverb and points out Burton's change of 'facundus' to 'jucundus'.

accuracy_reason: Aeneid 10.763–5 compares Mezentius to Orion and reads 'quam magnus Orion' and 'scindens'.
usefulness_reason: It gives the original context of the simile and shows how Burton adapts it to his giants.

accuracy_reason: The completion it gives matches Burton's own text.
usefulness_reason: It only repeats the Latin and English that come straight after the passage.

accuracy_reason: Cicero, Philippics 2.65, quotes 'male parta male dilabuntur' as the words of an unnamed poet, probably Naevius, so it is a line of verse.
usefulness_reason: Placing the jingle in Cicero is worth knowing, but the note gives no locus and is very brief.

accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.168 is quoted correctly. The note hedges its suggestion about where the Seneca sidenote belongs ('probably').
usefulness_reason: It names the Juvenal echo about Alexander and helps the reader place the sidenote.

accuracy_reason: It is a proverbial saying. It is related to the old monastic saying that a monk out of his cell is like a fish out of water.
usefulness_reason: Correct, but the note gives no origin or context.

accuracy_reason: Burton's English does add 'to live at home' to Pliny's sentence (NH 16.1.4).
usefulness_reason: Pointing out how Burton bends the phrase is useful, but the note does not name Pliny as the source.

accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.646: Anchises refuses to leave burning Troy.
usefulness_reason: It identifies the Virgilian source and the speaker, which gives the phrase its force here.

accuracy_reason: It is a well-known proverb.
usefulness_reason: A single word that tells most readers nothing new.

accuracy_reason: Giulio Cesare Barricelli wrote a book called Hortus genialis (1620), and Burton cites it in the ablative.
usefulness_reason: Naming the author and the book helps, but the part about the ablative is a grammar note.

accuracy_reason: 'Compescunt' does mean 'check' or 'restrain', and 'presently' meant 'immediately' in early modern English.
usefulness_reason: The gloss on 'presently' prevents a misreading, but the rest is about word choice.

accuracy_reason: Martial 11.16.9–10 is cited correctly, and the standard text does read 'leget'.
usefulness_reason: It gives the locus, and the variant reading makes the joke clear: she will read the book once Brutus leaves.

accuracy_reason: Leone Ebreo's Dialoghi do discuss intellectual or rational love. I cannot confirm that he uses the exact term 'amor cognitionis', which may come from a Latin version, so the claim is stated too firmly.
usefulness_reason: Identifying 'Leon' is useful, but the note adds little else.

accuracy_reason: The reading is offered with hedges ('may mean', 'seems likely'), and the note claims nothing it cannot support.
usefulness_reason: A tentative reading that helps a little with an obscure tag but does not trace it to Solinus.

accuracy_reason: The definition of 'parentare' is correct.
usefulness_reason: It explains a Roman ritual term that Burton applies to friends' commemorations.

accuracy_reason: The sentence does continue in 'veraciter amicus esse hominis…', and Burton's English gloss covers the whole of it.
usefulness_reason: A working note about how the passage is split, not about what it means.

accuracy_reason: The note's reading is plausible: the clause continues the series of 'alius' examples after the Aelian statue story, and 'ne qua pars probro vacet' leads into the next sentence.
usefulness_reason: Mostly a note on syntax and how the passage is split; the Bona Dea gloss adds little.

accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.204: Aeneas says 'horresco referens' as he tells how the serpents came over the sea for Laocoön.
usefulness_reason: Identifies the Virgilian allusion and its setting, and notes that Burton breaks it off.

accuracy_reason: Plutarch's Amatorius is set around Ismenodora's carrying off of the youth Bacchon, which matches Burton's sidenote 'In amatorio'.
usefulness_reason: Gives the source and the story behind Burton's brief allusion.

accuracy_reason: Burton's couplet does leave out the trembling and the 'breath of seething desire'.
usefulness_reason: Compares Burton's verse rendering with the Latin; a translator's note.

accuracy_reason: Aristotle states the mirror-clouding belief in De insomniis 459b, while Burton cites the Problems.
usefulness_reason: Explains the belief and corrects the locus Burton gives.

accuracy_reason: The text does read 'thorosaque brachia', split across two passages.
usefulness_reason: A note on how the passage is split.

accuracy_reason: Ovid, Met. 1.527–8, Daphne fleeing Apollo.
usefulness_reason: Repeats what Burton's own lead-in sentence already says.

accuracy_reason: Plotinus, Enneads 3.5.3, derives erōs from horasis (sight).
usefulness_reason: A correct gloss, but Burton's sentence already gives the etymology.

accuracy_reason: Heroides 12, Medea to Jason, recalling the moment she first saw him.
usefulness_reason: Adds the dramatic situation, but the sidenote already gives the source.

accuracy_reason: Gelasimus is the hungry parasite in Plautus' Stichus, and the name comes from Greek gelasimos, 'laughable'; the reading of 'de monte aureo' as a mock title is a fair interpretation.
usefulness_reason: Explains a comic name a reader would not recognize.

accuracy_reason: It is a proverbial tag, and Burton introduces it with 'as they say'.
usefulness_reason: Correct but slight; Burton's 'as they say' already marks it as a proverb.

accuracy_reason: The violas/violentius/violas/violenta wordplay is correctly described, and Burton's English (Violets, violent, violate) does keep it.
usefulness_reason: It points out a pun the reader would partly see anyway, and it doesn't name the source (Pontanus).

accuracy_reason: The phrase does continue the sentence attributed to Haedus ('Summo studio parentur epulae (saith Haedus)').
usefulness_reason: It only repeats what the text already shows.

accuracy_reason: Burton gives this as the subject of Astyanassa's writing, citing Suidas, and concubitus does mean sexual intercourse.
usefulness_reason: A correct but slight gloss.

accuracy_reason: These are Phaedra's words in Seneca's Phaedra (103–104). Pallas presides over weaving, and pensa is the allotted wool.
usefulness_reason: It glosses usefully, but it leaves out Seneca as the source.

accuracy_reason: The lines are a Latin version of an Anacreontic ode (the 'I would be your mirror' poem).
usefulness_reason: Burton already names Anacreon, and the note doesn't say which ode it is or who made the Latin.

accuracy_reason: 'John come kiss me now' was a well-known English tune and song of the period.
usefulness_reason: Identifying the tune is useful context, but the note is brief and partly a working remark.

accuracy_reason: It rightly ties the note, with suitable hedging, to the Latin rendering of Mimnermus fr. 1 (originally Greek).
usefulness_reason: It explains the bare sidenote, but only slightly.

accuracy_reason: In Memorabilia 1.3.13, Socrates advises Critobulus to stay away for a year (Xenophon himself is told to flee). Xenophon wrote in Greek.
usefulness_reason: Useful but slight; the sidenote already gives the locus.

accuracy_reason: In Calcagnini's dialogue, Galatea does complain of Triton's fickleness, and the main text paraphrases it loosely.
usefulness_reason: It connects the sidenote to the main text, which is modestly helpful.

accuracy_reason: It accurately describes how the passage is marked off and identifies Platina's dialogue on love.
usefulness_reason: This is mostly a working note about where the passage is marked.

accuracy_reason: The phrase does close Burton's list of authorities.
usefulness_reason: It repeats what is plain from the text.

accuracy_reason: The gloss of exuviae is right, and the reading of 'exuviae noctis' is properly hedged.
usefulness_reason: It helps with an obscure phrase but doesn't identify the source (Leech, 'Leochaeus').

accuracy_reason: 'Vita jugata' does mean married, yoked life, and the quotation does break off at 'Me juvat, &c.'
usefulness_reason: Explaining 'jugata' helps a little, but the remark that the quotation breaks off only repeats the '&c.'

accuracy_reason: Valerius Maximus (7.2 ext. 1) reports that Socrates, asked whether a man should marry, answered that he would repent whichever he did.
usefulness_reason: It links Burton's line to the classical story behind his sidenote.

accuracy_reason: These are the opening lines of Terence's Adelphoe: Micio calls his slave Storax and worries about Aeschinus, his adopted son.
usefulness_reason: It names the speaker and situation but not the play or Terence, which is what the reader most needs.

accuracy_reason: The line is a play on sounds (lacerat/lacertum/Largi), and 'lacertus' is the upper arm.
usefulness_reason: It points out wordplay that a reader of the English loses, but it says little else.

accuracy_reason: The phrase does finish Erasmus's clause, which begins 'Melius sic errare, quam zelotypiae curis'.
usefulness_reason: A translator's note on syntax.

accuracy_reason: The lines scan as a hexameter followed by a pentameter, so they are an elegiac couplet, and the main text gives the gist as 'such a mother, such a daughter'.
usefulness_reason: Naming the metre and pointing back to the proverb is accurate but slight.

accuracy_reason: 'Aliud agere' is a standard Latin idiom for attending to something other than what one should.
usefulness_reason: It explains the idiom briefly, and the translation already conveys most of it.

accuracy_reason: Burton does render 'ob metum publicae potestatis' loosely as 'for fear of Laws'.
usefulness_reason: A working note comparing Burton's English with the Latin.

accuracy_reason: Socinians did make right reason the norm for interpreting Scripture.
usefulness_reason: Burton already names the Socinians, so the note adds only a little context.

accuracy_reason: In Discourses II.2 Machiavelli argues that Christianity has made men weak, and the note is right to hedge on where the Latin comes from (Burton likely used the Latin translation of the Discourses).
usefulness_reason: It gives the source, explains how the Latin relates to it, and adds a useful shade of meaning.

accuracy_reason: The phrase does continue Burton's quotation from Josephus that begins 'exertos praebentes jugulos'.
usefulness_reason: A working note on how the passage joins up, and it doesn't give the Josephus passage.

accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Nero 38, tells how someone quoted 'When I am dead, let earth be mingled with fire' and Nero answered 'No, while I live'; the original is in Greek.
usefulness_reason: It names the source of the anecdote and explains how Burton's Latin relates to the Greek.

accuracy_reason: The lines are Ovid, Amores 3.9.35–36, the elegy on Tibullus, and the standard text does read 'Cum rapiunt'.
usefulness_reason: It names the exact poem and points out Burton's variant.

accuracy_reason: The sidenote points to Chrysostom's homily on Ephesians, and the description of the passage fits.
usefulness_reason: It names the speaker but adds little beyond what the context already shows.

accuracy_reason: It correctly completes Justin's sentence (book 20) as Burton quotes it.
usefulness_reason: It only joins up and retranslates the sentence that is already in the text.

accuracy_reason: Contraventio is a late or medieval Latin word. Acting against one's scruples was the casuists' standard remedy, and the note hedges this properly.
usefulness_reason: The casuistry context is useful, but the punctuation remark is a translator's working note.

accuracy_reason: The reading follows Agrippa's 'lapides loquimur' image of hard sayings as stones that could knock out a reader's brains.
usefulness_reason: It explains the image but does not give Agrippa's source passage or how Burton adapts it.

accuracy_reason: This is the closing sentence of the Phaedo, and there Phaedo addresses Echecrates.
usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and corrects Burton's 'Eucrates'.

accuracy_reason: Quintilian, Institutio 2.12, does attack frenzied declaimers, and the remark about the garbled syntax is suitably hedged.
usefulness_reason: It gives the context and helps with the construction, but adds little else.

accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.3.50–51, reads 'hic dextrorsum abit … partibus' without 'omnes', just as the note says.
usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and shows how Burton changes it, though it gives no exact line reference.

accuracy_reason: The meanings given for privus and privatus are correct.
usefulness_reason: The gloss on the wordplay is slight but helpful.

accuracy_reason: Cicero, In Catilinam 1.30, has 'tam adultam rei publicae pestem', and the identification is hedged properly.
usefulness_reason: It points out a likely Ciceronian echo and how Burton changes it.

accuracy_reason: The quotation is Juvenal 10.188, and Seneca, Letter 10.5, does read 'hominem'. 'The rest' is a little loose, since the opening 'O Jupiter contingat…' clause is not Seneca's.
usefulness_reason: It separates the two sources and records Burton's variant.

accuracy_reason: The infinitive is indeed reported speech.
usefulness_reason: It is a grammar note for the translator.

accuracy_reason: Burton does give the Latin as an alternative to 'supervisors', and praefecti aerarii were indeed Roman officers of the public treasury (the aerarium Saturni).
usefulness_reason: It gives brief Roman context for the title but adds little to the translation.

accuracy_reason: Theognis 230 does read χρήματά τοι θνητοῖς γίγνεται ἀφροσύνη, and Burton's τοῖς is a variant or corruption; his Latin rendering does follow in the same sidenote.
usefulness_reason: The line reference is helpful, but the rest is mostly a textual note about the particle.
